deep.reconstruction:
Setting: p ≡ 1 (mod 3) prime, x a primitive p-th root of unity, R a complex primitive cube root of unity (later written ρ), g a primitive root mod p, f a root of f^3 ≡ 1 (mod p), f ≢ 1. The three 'Klassen' are the cubic-residue cosets C_j = {g^{3k+j}}.

(A) The product problem (top of page). Gauss forms the 'partial resolvent' F_α = x^α + R x^{αf} + R^2 x^{αf^2} for α in the first class. He then takes the product Π = ∏_α F_α over the (p−1)/3 values of α.

He compares Π with the cubic Lagrange resolvent / cubic Gauss sum P = Σ_k (x^{g^{3k}} + R x^{g^{3k+1}} + R^2 x^{g^{3k+2}}) = η0 + Rη1 + R^2η2, where η_j are the cubic periods. In character language P = Σ_n ψ(n) x^n with ψ(g) = R.

Claim: Π = P·M with M a rational function of R, i.e. M ∈ Q(ρ).

Why this holds (my filling-in): F_{αf} = R^{-1} F_α. So Π depends only on the cosets α<f>, up to a power of R, and the first class is a full set of coset representatives. Write σ_c for x → x^c.
- For a cube c, σ_c permutes the factors.
- σ_g sends C0 to C1 = f^{±1}C0. Hence σ_g Π = R^{-(p-1)/3·(±1)} Π = R^{-1} Π, the same eigenvalue as P (σ_g P = R^{-1} P).
- The R^{-1}-eigenspace of Gal(Q(ζ_p)/Q) acting on Q(ρ)(ζ_p) is one-dimensional over Q(ρ), spanned by P. Hence Π = M P with M = Π·P̄/p ∈ Q(ρ).

This is the exact cubic analogue of the quadratic product ∏_{k=1}^{(p-1)/2} (x^k − x^{-k}), which Gauss used in 1805 to fix the sign of the quadratic Gauss sum. Here f = −1 is replaced by a cube root of 1 mod p.

Table of results: p=7: M = R; p=13: M = 2+R; p=19: M = 2+4R+5R^2 (= −3−R). The norms are 1, 3, 7.

My check, p=7 (g=3, f=2): (x+Rx^2+R^2x^4)(x^6+Rx^5+R^2x^3) = R(x+x^6) + R^2(x^3+x^4) + (x^2+x^5) = R·P. This is exactly M = R.

My check, p=13 (g=2, f=3, α ∈ {1,5,8,12}): with a_k = x^k + x^{-k},
- F1F12 = R a2 + R^2 a5 + a6;
- F5F8 = R a3 + R^2 a1 + a4;
- the product is (1+2R^2)η0 + (2+R)η1 + (2R+R^2)η2 = (R^2−R)·P.
Note R^2 − R = R^2(2+R). So Gauss's M = 2+R is confirmed up to the unit R^2, which depends on his unrecorded choice of g, f and representatives. The norm 3 agrees.

p=19: not checked by hand.

(B) Arithmetic in Z[ρ] (lower half).

Translations: √−3 = 1+2ρ, so
- 1+√−3 = 2+2ρ = 1+ρ−ρ^2;
- 2+√−3 = 3+2ρ = 2+ρ−ρ^2;
- 2−√−3 = 1−2ρ = 3+2ρ^2.
The last two are prime factors of 7.

Sketch: lattice points 0, −1, √−3, −1+√−3, 2+√−3 with intersecting arcs. Separately, a rhombus (60°/120° parallelogram), presumably a fundamental cell of the lattice Z[ρ] or of a sublattice πZ[ρ]. The next page has a hexagonal 'Schema für 43'.

Tables of the cubic classes modulo a prime π of norm p, using small Eisenstein integers as representatives. Columns are the classes C0, C1, C2.
- p=7, π = 2−ρ (ρ ≡ 2): columns {1,−1} ≡ {1,6}, {−ρ^2, ρ^2} ≡ {3,4}, {ρ,−ρ} ≡ {2,5}. These are exactly the cubic classes mod 7.
- p=13, π = 3−ρ (ρ ≡ 3): columns {1, 1−ρ^2, −1, −1+ρ^2} ≡ {1,5,12,8} = cubes; {1−ρ, ρ, −1+ρ, −ρ} ≡ {11,3,2,10} = C1; the third column ≡ {4,7,9,6} = C2. All correct.
- p=19, π = 3−2ρ (ρ ≡ 11, ρ^2 ≡ 7): rows are row1 = (1, 1−ρ, 2ρ^2) multiplied by the units 1, −ρ^2, ρ, −1. The residues are {1,12,11,18} ⊂ C0, {9,13,4,10} ⊂ C2, {14,16,2,5} ⊂ C1. All correct, but only 4 of the 6 rows are written.

Prime list p = N(π): 31 = N(5−ρ), 37 = N(4−3ρ), 43 = N(6−ρ), 61 = N(5−4ρ), 67 = N(7−2ρ), 73 = N(8−ρ). The next page continues with 79 = N(7−3ρ).

Character column headed 8−ρ (p = 73, ρ ≡ 8): next to ρ, 1−ρ, 2, 2−ρ, 3−ρ, 3−2ρ, 5, 5−ρ stand the values 0,0,2,2,1,2,1,0. I verified that each value v satisfies a^{24} ≡ ρ^v (mod 8−ρ). These are cubic residue characters (indices) of the small primes and units modulo the prime 8−ρ, i.e. a table of the cubic residue symbol.
errors: p=13: under the natural convention (g=2, f=3=g^4, α ∈ cubes) the multiplier comes out as R^2−R = R^2·(2+R), not 2+R. This is a unit-factor discrepancy, explicable by a different choice of g, f or coset representatives. It is not a substantive error, but the exact normalization is not reproducible from the page.
p=19 value M = 2+4R+5R^2 (= −3−R, norm 7) was not verified by hand; flagged for CAS check (up to a unit).
The p=19 class table lists only 4 of the (p−1)/3 = 6 rows (the multipliers ρ^2 and −ρ are missing), so it is incomplete rather than wrong.

The quantifier 'α ... der ersten Klasse' is ambiguous. On the previous page 'Klassen' (for p=13, 19) are not the cubic-residue cosets. The product is in any case only defined up to a power of R unless α runs over a fixed set of representatives of the cosets of <f>.

results.what: The product over representatives α of cosets of <f> (f^3≡1 mod p) of x^α + R x^{αf} + R^2 x^{αf^2} equals P·M, with P the cubic Gauss sum (Lagrange resolvent) and M ∈ Q(ρ). Explicit M for p = 7, 13, 19.
results.modern_name: Cubic analogue of Gauss's product formula for the quadratic Gauss sum (sign determination); Galois-eigenspace argument for cubic Gauss sums; related to Kummer's cubic Gauss sum problem and Stickelberger-type factorizations
results.usually_credited_to: Quadratic case Gauss (1805/1811); cubic Gauss sums studied by Kummer (1842/46), Jacobi, Eisenstein

results.what: Factorization of primes p ≡ 1 mod 3 as norms of Eisenstein integers (7, 13, 19, 31, 37, 43, 61, 67, 73) and conversion between a+b√−3 and ρ-forms
Representatives of the three cubic residue classes mod π (N(π) = 7, 13, 19) by small Eisenstein integers (units and unit multiples)
results.modern_name: Cubic residue classes modulo a prime of Z[ω]

results.what: Table of cubic characters of ρ, 1−ρ, 2, 2−ρ, 3−ρ, 3−2ρ, 5, 5−ρ modulo π = 8−ρ (norm 73); values = exponent v with a^{(N−1)/3} ≡ ρ^v
results.modern_name: Cubic residue symbol (a/π)_3; data for cubic reciprocity and supplementary laws

deep.surprise_reason: Gauss's work on cubic residues and Eisenstein integers is documented in his Nachlass, so the lower half is routine for him. The upper half is a less known detail. In 1805, the year he settled the sign of the quadratic Gauss sum through the product ∏(x^k − x^{-k}), he tried the direct cubic analogue and found that the product equals the cubic Gauss sum times a non-unit factor M ∈ Z[ρ] (norms 1, 3, 7). This is a notable unpublished experiment on the cubic Gauss sum problem later associated with Kummer. It records no general theorem, and the proportionality itself follows from a simple eigenspace argument.

checkable.asserts: p=7 (g=3, f=2): the product equals R·P, i.e. M = R
p=13 (g=2, f=3): the product equals R^2(2+R)·P, i.e. Gauss's M = 2+R up to the unit R^2
p=19 (g=2, f=7): one entry should be 0 if Gauss's M = 2+4R+5R^2 is correct up to a unit
N(a−bρ) = a^2+ab+b^2 with ρ → −ρ convention, i.e. norms of 2−ρ, 3−ρ, 3−2ρ, 5−ρ, 4−3ρ, 6−ρ, 5−4ρ, 7−2ρ, 8−ρ
Cubic characters mod 8−ρ (ρ≡8, 8^2=64): values 0,0,2,2,1,2,1,0 as written
p=13, π=3−ρ (ρ≡3): first column {1, 1−ρ^2, −1, −1+ρ^2} is the set of cubic residues
p=19, π=3−2ρ (ρ≡11, ρ^2≡7): third column {2ρ^2, −2ρ, 2, −2ρ^2} lies in class C1

transcription_corrections: '7 | [-2-]ρ' should read '7 | 2−ρ' (the modulus of norm 7; ρ ≡ 2 mod it).
In the p=19 table, row 3 col 1 '−4ρ' should be '+ρ' (row 3 = ρ·row 1: ρ, ρ−ρρ, 2); −4ρ ≡ 13 is not a cubic residue.
The column headed '8−ρ' with values 0,0,2,2,1,2,1,0 is a table of cubic characters modulo 8−ρ (N = 73), not a continuation of the 31 entry.
'1+ρ−ρρ' is just 1+√−3 rewritten (√−3 = 1+2ρ). '2+ρ−ρρ' and '3+2ρρ' (= 1−2ρ) are 2+√−3 and 2−√−3; these readings are consistent, so the '[?]' marks can be removed.
'7 und 29' is doubtful (29 ≢ 1 mod 3); possibly '7 und 19'.
